listeningParts.title: Booking a bug hotel workshop
listeningParts.contextDescription: A parent phones a nature centre to book places on a children's workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Hello, Riverside Nature Centre, Ben speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I saw that you're running a bug hotel workshop for children, and I'd like to book places for my two kids, if there's still room.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, we've got a few sessions coming up. They're all on Saturday mornings. Which date were you interested in?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: I was hoping for the tenth of May.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Let me have a look. I'm afraid the tenth is completely full. It's been very popular. But there are still places on the seventeenth. Would that work?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: The seventeenth. Yes, I think so. We're not doing anything that weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Great. Can I take your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: It's Joanna Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And how old are the children? The workshop is designed for ages six to twelve.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That's fine. My daughter's seven and my son is ten.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Perfect. Now, the price. For members of the centre, it's six pounds per child, and for non-members it's eight pounds. Are you members?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: No, we're not, although we've been meaning to join for ages.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Well, if you join on the day, we can take the difference off your membership fee. Adults come free, by the way, and you're very welcome to stay and help.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Oh, I'd love to. Could you tell me a bit about what they'll actually do?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. A bug hotel is a kind of shelter that gives insects and other small creatures somewhere to live, especially over the winter. Each child builds their own small one, using a wooden frame, which we provide. They fill it with natural materials. We use pine cones, dry leaves, pieces of bark and hollow bamboo canes. Solitary bees, for example, like to lay their eggs inside the bamboo tubes, and ladybirds often spend the winter hidden among the pine cones.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: That sounds lovely. Can they bring it home?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, each child takes home their bug hotel, along with a leaflet about garden insects, so they can identify who moves in. We suggest putting it somewhere sheltered, facing the sun, about a metre off the ground.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: And where do we meet?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The workshop takes place in the wooden barn next to the car park, not in the main visitor centre. It starts at ten and finishes at twelve thirty.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Is there somewhere to park? We'll probably drive, because it's quite a long way from our house.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, parking is free for visitors, but it does fill up quickly on Saturdays, so I'd suggest arriving by about a quarter to ten. There's also a café in the visitor centre if you'd like a coffee while you wait, and the children get a drink and a biscuit halfway through the session.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Is there anything they need to bring?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We provide gloves and all the tools, but they should wear old clothes, because it can get messy. And part of the session is outside collecting materials, so I'd recommend boots, as the ground near the river is often muddy.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Good to know. Oh, one thing I should mention. My son has quite bad hay fever. He's allergic to grass. Will that be a problem?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thanks for telling me. I'll make a note for the leader. Most of the outdoor part is in the woodland, rather than the meadow, so it shouldn't be too bad, but he might want to bring his medicine just in case.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: I'll make sure he does. And is there anything else happening that day?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's an optional pond-dipping session in the afternoon, starting at quarter past two, where children can look at water insects like dragonfly larvae and water boatmen. It's free for anyone who's done the morning workshop.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: Brilliant, we might stay for that. How do I pay?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You can pay on the day. Just one last question for our records: how did you find out about the workshop?

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.text: It was in the school newsletter last week.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely, thank you. So that's two places on Saturday the seventeenth. We look forward to seeing you.

listeningParts.title: A meadow for pollinators
listeningParts.contextDescription: A park manager talks to local residents about a new wildflower area in a city park.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming. My name's Leah Moretti, and I manage Ashgrove Park for the city council. Tonight I want to explain our plans to turn part of the park into a wildflower area for pollinators, and to answer any questions you have.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: So, first of all, why are we doing this? When people hear the word 'pollinator', they usually think of honeybees. But in fact, a huge range of insects carry pollen from flower to flower, including bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies, butterflies, moths and even some beetles. Many of these insects have declined in recent decades, and one of the main reasons is the loss of the flower-rich grasslands they depend on. Parks like ours can't solve that problem on their own, but they can provide important stepping stones for insects moving through the city.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, I know that some of you are worried about how this will look. At the moment, the area by the eastern gate is just short grass that we mow every week in summer. Under the new plan, we'll mow that area much less often. Some people have told me they think this will look untidy or neglected. What we're going to do is keep a mown strip, about two metres wide, along the edges and paths. That shows people that the long grass is deliberate, and in our experience, it makes a big difference to how people feel about it.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We'll cut the meadow itself just once a year, in late summer, after the flowers have set seed. And this is important: we'll remove the cuttings rather than leaving them on the ground. That might seem strange, but most wildflowers actually grow best in poor soil. If the cuttings rot down, they add nutrients, and then fast-growing grasses take over and crowd out the flowers.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The project is being paid for by a grant from a wildlife charity, so it won't cost residents anything extra. We'll be relying on volunteers, though, especially for planting in the autumn, so if you're interested, please leave your details on the sheet at the back.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me tell you about some of the plants we're including, because each one has a particular job. Near the entrance, we're planting willow. Its catkins appear very early in spring, and they're one of the first sources of pollen for queen bumblebees coming out of hibernation. Along the old wall, we'll let the ivy grow. People often think of ivy as a weed, but it flowers in autumn, when hardly anything else does, so it's a vital source of food for insects late in the year.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: In the corner by the compost bins, we're deliberately leaving a patch of stinging nettles. I know they're not very popular with dog walkers! But they're the main food plant for the caterpillars of several butterflies, such as the peacock and the small tortoiseshell. In the main flower bed, we'll have foxgloves. Their flowers are long tubes, so they suit bumblebees with long tongues that can reach the nectar deep inside. And finally, we're planting fennel. Its flat clusters of tiny flowers are very popular with hoverflies, which are excellent pollinators and whose larvae also eat aphids, so they help gardeners too.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: We're also being careful about where our seeds come from. Rather than buying a cheap mixture that might include plants from other parts of the world, we're using seed collected from wildflower meadows in this region. Local plants are better suited to our soil and climate, and the insects here are adapted to them. It does cost a little more, but we think it's worth it.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: To find out whether the project's working, we'll be running insect counts three times a year, in May, July and September, and anyone can join in. You don't need to be an expert; we'll give you an identification guide and a short training session. The results will be published on the council's website. Right, I'll stop there. Does anyone have any questions?

listeningParts.title: Planning a campus insect survey
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two biology students, Megan and Tom, talk to their tutor about an insect survey project.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Megan, Tom. So, you've decided to do your project on insects on the campus. Tell me what you're planning.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Well, the basic question is whether different types of habitat on campus support different numbers and types of insects. We've chosen three sites: the short grass on the main lawn, the wildflower strip behind the library, and the small wood near the sports hall.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good, that gives you a nice contrast. What made you choose this topic?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Partly the news stories about insect decline. But mainly, the university's just started managing some areas for wildlife, and the grounds team said they'd like some data to see whether it's making a difference.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's excellent, because it means your project could actually be useful. How are you going to collect the insects?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: We're using two methods. For insects on the ground, mainly beetles and spiders, we'll use pitfall traps. They're just plastic cups sunk into the soil so the rim is level with the surface. Anything walking along falls in.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Are you going to put any liquid in them?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We talked about that. Some studies use a preservative, but that kills everything. We'd rather keep the insects alive, identify them, and release them. So we'll leave the cups dry, and check them every twenty-four hours, because otherwise the predators, like the larger beetles, start eating the other insects.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sensible. And make sure you put a cover over each one, a little raised above the cup, or they'll fill with water when it rains.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Yes, we were going to use small squares of wood for that.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the second method?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: A moth trap. It's a box with a bright light on top that attracts moths at night. They fall into the box and settle among egg trays inside, and in the morning we identify and release them. The ecology department has agreed to lend us one.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Have you checked that you're allowed to put traps on university land?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Yes, the grounds team were happy for us to go ahead. We just have to mark each trap with a small flag, so that the gardeners don't mow over them or trip on them, and we've filled in a risk assessment form for working outside at night.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. That's exactly the kind of thing examiners like to see mentioned.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Where will you run it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That's a problem, actually. We'd planned to put it in all three sites, but the main lawn is next to the student halls, and we were worried the light would disturb people trying to sleep. So we'll only use it in the wood and behind the library.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's fine, as long as you explain why in your methods section. It does mean you can't compare all three sites for moths, so be careful about the conclusions you draw. How often are you sampling?

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Once a week for six weeks, in June and early July.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how will you deal with the weather? Moth numbers can vary enormously depending on temperature.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We hadn't really thought about that. I suppose we could record the temperature each night?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, record the minimum overnight temperature, and also wind and cloud cover, because moths fly much less on clear, cold nights. And try to run the trap on the same nights at both sites, so that the weather is the same for each.

dialogue.speaker: Megan
dialogue.text: Good idea. The other thing we're unsure about is identification. Some of the beetles are really hard to tell apart.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Don't try to identify everything to species level. For the difficult groups, it's perfectly acceptable to sort them into families. You'll still be able to compare the sites. And take good photographs, so that an expert can check them later if necessary.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Should we share our results with anyone?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Definitely. Send a summary to the grounds team, and you could also submit your records to the national recording website, so they become part of the wider scientific data. Right, I'd like to see a draft of your methods section in two weeks.

listeningParts.title: The science of fireflies
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a biology course about how fireflies produce light and why they are under threat.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're looking at one of the most magical sights in the natural world: fireflies. On summer evenings in many parts of the world, fields and forests light up with thousands of tiny flashing lights. But how do these insects produce light, why do they do it, and why are scientists worried about their future?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let's start with some basic facts. Despite their name, fireflies aren't flies at all. They're beetles, belonging to a family called the Lampyridae, and there are more than two thousand known species. They're found on every continent except Antarctica, but they're most diverse in warm, humid regions of Asia and the Americas. In some places, people call them lightning bugs.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The production of light by living things is called bioluminescence. In fireflies, it takes place in special light organs, usually near the end of the abdomen. Inside these organs, a chemical called luciferin reacts with oxygen. The reaction is made possible by an enzyme called luciferase, and it also requires a molecule called ATP, which is the main energy carrier in living cells. What's remarkable is how efficient this reaction is. An ordinary old-fashioned light bulb loses most of its energy as heat, but almost all the energy from the firefly's reaction is released as light. That's why it's sometimes described as cold light.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So how does a firefly switch its light on and off? The answer seems to lie in controlling the supply of oxygen to the light organ. Researchers have found evidence that a gas called nitric oxide plays a role in this, allowing oxygen to reach the light-producing cells in short bursts. That's what creates the flash.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, why do they flash? In most species, the main purpose is courtship. Typically, males fly around flashing a particular pattern, and females, waiting on the ground or on plants, respond with their own flash. Each species has its own code, which might differ in the length of the flash, the number of flashes, or the time between them. This allows fireflies to find partners of the right species in the dark.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: But this system can be exploited. Females of some species in a group called Photuris have learned to copy the flash responses of females of other species. When a male of the other species arrives, expecting to find a mate, the Photuris female catches and eats him. Scientists sometimes call them femme fatale fireflies. And by eating these males, they also gain chemicals that help protect them from their own predators, such as spiders.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: It's not only adults that glow. Firefly larvae produce light too, and in many species, the glow seems to act as a warning to predators that they taste unpleasant. The larvae live on the ground or in leaf litter, and they're fierce predators themselves. Many feed on snails and slugs, injecting them with digestive chemicals that turn their prey into a liquid.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the most extraordinary displays happens in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park in the United States, where one species flashes in unison. Thousands of males flash together, then go dark together, creating waves of light through the forest. It's become so popular that the park now uses a lottery system to limit the number of visitors. Similar synchronised displays occur in mangrove forests in Southeast Asia.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Sadly, there's growing evidence that many firefly populations are declining. A major review by firefly experts identified three main threats. The first is the loss of habitat, as wetlands, meadows and forests are cleared for building and agriculture. The second is light pollution. Artificial lights from streets and buildings make it harder for fireflies to see each other's signals, and so they find mates less successfully. The third is the use of pesticides, which can kill both the adults and the larvae.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, fireflies have also made an important contribution to science. Scientists have learned to insert the gene for luciferase into other organisms, so that cells glow when a particular gene is active. This technique is now widely used in medical research. In the next session, we'll look at other bioluminescent organisms, particularly those in the deep ocean.

readingPassages.title: The monarch butterfly's great journey
paragraphs: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies in eastern North America begin one of the most remarkable journeys in the animal kingdom. Leaving southern Canada and the northern United States, they fly south for more than three thousand kilometres to spend the winter in a small area of mountain forest in central Mexico. No other butterfly is known to make such a long, regular two-way migration, and for many years the question of where these insects actually went was one of the great mysteries of natural history.

The answer was found through the persistence of a Canadian zoologist, Fred Urquhart, who began studying monarch migration in the late 1930s. From the 1950s onwards, he and his wife Norah organised thousands of volunteers to attach tiny paper labels to the wings of monarchs, each with a request that anyone finding the butterfly should report it. Gradually, the reports pointed towards Mexico. Finally, in January 1975, two of their collaborators, Ken Brugger and Catalina Aguado, found the overwintering sites high in the mountains west of Mexico City. The discovery was announced to the world in National Geographic magazine in 1976.

The sites are as extraordinary as the journey. The butterflies gather in dense clusters on the trunks and branches of oyamel fir trees, at altitudes of around three thousand metres. So many butterflies may settle on a single tree that branches have been known to break under their weight. The cool mountain climate allows the monarchs to survive the winter in a state of low activity, using up their stored fat slowly, while the forest canopy protects them from the worst of the cold and from rain and snow. The butterflies remain there until the days lengthen and temperatures rise in late winter, when they begin to mate and prepare to leave.

One of the most surprising facts about the migration is that no single butterfly completes the whole round trip. Monarchs born in early summer live for only a few weeks as adults. The generation that flies south in autumn, however, is different: these butterflies do not breed until the following spring, and they can live for up to eight months. In spring, they fly north to the southern United States, where they lay their eggs and die. It then takes several more generations, each living only a few weeks, to recolonise the north.

How the butterflies find their way to a place they have never visited remains a subject of research. Experiments have shown that monarchs use the position of the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, they must also keep track of time, and scientists have discovered that the internal clocks that allow them to do this are located partly in their antennae. There is also evidence that monarchs can use the Earth's magnetic field to help them navigate, which may be particularly useful on cloudy days.

Monarchs are closely linked to a single group of plants. Their caterpillars feed only on milkweeds, which contain poisonous chemicals. The caterpillars are not harmed by these chemicals; instead, they store them in their bodies, and the poisons remain in the adult butterflies. This makes monarchs unpleasant to eat, and many birds learn to avoid them after a single attempt. The butterflies' bright orange and black colouring acts as a warning, advertising to predators that they are not worth attacking.

Unfortunately, the eastern monarch population has declined dramatically. Because the butterflies cluster so tightly together, scientists estimate the population by measuring the area of forest they occupy in winter. In the mid-1990s, the colonies covered around eighteen hectares; in the winter of 2013 to 2014, they covered less than one hectare. Several causes have been identified. The most important is thought to be the loss of milkweed in the United States, much of it due to the increased use of herbicides on farmland. Illegal logging in Mexico and extreme weather events have also played a part.

Efforts to protect the monarch now involve all three countries along its route. In Mexico, the overwintering area is protected as the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, which was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. In the United States and Canada, governments, schools and individual gardeners have been encouraged to plant milkweed and other flowers that provide nectar for adult butterflies. Whether these efforts will be enough to secure the future of this extraordinary migration is not yet clear, but they show how a single insect can inspire cooperation across an entire continent.

readingPassages.title: Farmers in miniature
paragraphs: Humans began farming around ten thousand years ago, and the change transformed our species. Yet we were not the first farmers on Earth. Tens of millions of years earlier, certain groups of ants had already begun to cultivate their own food. The most famous of these are the leafcutter ants of Central and South America, whose long columns of workers, each carrying a piece of leaf above its head, are a familiar sight in tropical forests. For a long time, people assumed that the ants were simply collecting food to eat. The truth turned out to be far more surprising.

Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they collect. Instead, they carry them back to their underground nests, where smaller workers cut them into tiny pieces, chew them into a pulp and use the pulp to grow a fungus. The ants and their fungus depend completely on each other. The fungus produces small, nutrient-rich swellings that the ants harvest and feed to their larvae, while the fungus relies on the ants to supply it with fresh leaves, to protect it, and to carry it to new places. Neither can survive in the wild without the other.

A mature leafcutter colony is an enormous enterprise, and it can take several years to reach its full size. In some species, a single nest may contain several million workers and extend several metres below the ground, with hundreds of chambers connected by tunnels. The work is divided according to size. The largest workers defend the colony, medium-sized workers cut and carry leaves, and the smallest care for the fungus gardens. Some tiny workers even ride on the leaf fragments as they are carried home, where they appear to protect the carriers from parasitic flies that try to lay eggs on them.

Like human farmers, the ants must deal with pests. Their fungus gardens can be attacked by another fungus, called Escovopsis, which can destroy a garden if it is not controlled. In 1999, a team of researchers including Cameron Currie published a discovery that changed the way scientists thought about the ants. They found that the ants carry bacteria on their bodies which produce substances that kill or slow the growth of Escovopsis. In effect, the ants use antibiotics to protect their crops, something humans have only done for less than a century.

The ants are also careful about hygiene. Waste material from the fungus gardens, which may contain harmful organisms, is carried to special waste chambers or to heaps outside the nest. Studies have shown that the workers who handle this waste are kept separate from the rest of the colony. They rarely enter the fungus gardens, and if they try to, other workers may attack them. This strict division reduces the risk that disease will spread to the precious fungus on which the whole colony depends.

The beginning of a new colony depends on a single queen. Before she leaves her birth nest on her mating flight, a young queen places a small piece of the fungus in a pouch inside her mouth. After mating, she digs a small chamber in the soil, spits out the fungus and begins a new garden, which she feeds and tends herself until her first workers are old enough to take over. In this way, the same fungus has been passed down through countless generations of queens, rather like seeds saved from one harvest to plant the next.

Leafcutters are not the only insects that farm. Some termites in Africa and Asia also grow fungus in their mounds, and certain beetles, known as ambrosia beetles, cultivate fungus inside the tunnels they dig in wood. Many other ant species practise a form of animal farming. They tend groups of aphids, small insects that feed on plant sap, and collect the sweet liquid, known as honeydew, that the aphids produce. In return, the ants protect the aphids from predators such as ladybirds, and some even carry them to fresh plants.

These tiny farmers have much to teach us. Because leafcutter ants have managed to grow essentially a single crop for millions of years without it being wiped out by disease, some biologists believe that studying them may help us understand how to make human agriculture more resilient. Others are investigating the bacteria the ants use, in the hope of discovering new antibiotics. Ironically, in parts of Latin America, the same ants are regarded as serious agricultural pests, because a large colony can strip the leaves from crops and fruit trees in a single night.

readingPassages.title: Are the insects disappearing?
paragraphs: Many people over a certain age remember long summer drives after which the car windscreen was covered in dead insects. Today, they say, the windscreen stays almost clean. This so-called 'windscreen phenomenon' is only an anecdote, and it could be explained by other factors, such as the more streamlined shape of modern cars. But it reflects a growing fear among scientists and the public alike that insects are disappearing. Since the late 2010s, newspaper headlines have warned of an 'insect apocalypse'. The question is how far the evidence supports such dramatic language, and what, if anything, should be done about it.

Concern about the effect of human activity on insects is not new. In 1962, the American biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, which described how widespread use of pesticides was harming birds and other wildlife, and which helped to inspire the modern environmental movement. Twenty-five years later, the biologist E. O. Wilson famously described insects and other invertebrates as 'the little things that run the world', arguing that if they were to disappear, ecosystems would collapse, whereas the world would manage quite well without humans.

The study that brought the issue to wide public attention was published in 2017. For almost three decades, amateur entomologists from a society in the German town of Krefeld had used special tent-like traps to collect flying insects in nature reserves, mainly in western Germany. When the samples were analysed, they showed that the total weight of flying insects caught had fallen by more than three-quarters over twenty-seven years. What made the result so alarming was that the losses had occurred in protected areas, which were supposed to be refuges for wildlife.

Two years later, a review by the scientists Francisco Sánchez-Bayo and Kris Wyckhuys went further, suggesting that more than forty per cent of insect species could face extinction in the coming decades. This claim was widely reported, but it was also strongly criticised by other researchers. Critics pointed out that the authors had searched for studies using the word 'decline', which may have caused them to overlook studies showing stable or increasing populations, and that most of the data came from Europe and North America.

A more cautious picture emerged in 2020, when a team led by Roel van Klink combined data from more than 160 long-term studies around the world. They found that the number of land-dwelling insects was falling by around nine per cent per decade, a serious but less catastrophic rate than some headlines had suggested. Surprisingly, insects that live in fresh water, such as mayflies and midges, had increased, which the researchers linked to efforts to clean up rivers and lakes. In my view, this finding is one of the most encouraging in the whole debate, because it shows that environmental policies can work.

Why should we care? Insects carry out an enormous range of tasks on which humans depend. Around three-quarters of the world's major food crops benefit at least to some extent from animal pollination, most of it carried out by insects. Insects break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil, and they are food for countless birds, fish and other animals. Many insects also control pests: ladybirds and hoverfly larvae, for example, eat large numbers of aphids. A serious decline in insects would therefore have consequences far beyond the insects themselves.

The causes of decline are many, and they interact. The loss of natural habitats to farming and building is generally considered the most important. Pesticides, particularly insecticides, kill insects directly, while herbicides remove the wild plants on which many insects feed. Climate change, light pollution and invasive species add further pressures. In my view, it is a mistake to look for a single cause, as some campaigners do, because this encourages the belief that one simple solution, such as banning one type of chemical, would solve the problem.

What, then, should we conclude? The phrase 'insect apocalypse' is probably an exaggeration, and it risks damaging the credibility of scientists if the worst predictions do not come true. Yet the evidence that many insect populations are declining, especially in heavily farmed regions, is strong. In my view, the greatest problem is not exaggeration but ignorance: we have reliable long-term data for only a tiny fraction of the world's insects, and almost none for the tropics, where most species live. Monitoring insects properly, with the help of volunteers like those in Krefeld, should be a priority.
